_notes.change: Initial implementation. requireCodeOwnerReview=true enforces team reviewer requests via CODEOWNERS + this flag. The ruleset field required_reviewers is not available on the current GitHub plan.

Added 3 strict required checks for spark-match-02-infrastructure (tflint, gitleaks, sonar-terraform) after gap analysis revealed 3 PRs (#77/#78/#79) had bypassed tflint via admin-bypass. Tracked in tasks/devops/pending/sprint-2/03-strict-required-checks-and-admin-bypass-policy.md.

Reconciled spark-match-02-infrastructure statusChecks against actual reported check contexts. Manifest had 5 placeholder names (Plan (dev) / Plan (dev), tflint (env=dev), etc.) that did not match the 8 checks GitHub Actions actually reports (plan-dev / plan-, tflint / tflint-, etc.). Surfaced by --check returning drift. Fix: replaced 5 placeholders with the 8 real check contexts reported by /actions/runs/{id}/jobs API.

Added lint-commits / commitlint-main to required status checks for spark-match-01-devops. Defense against REST API merge pitfall: when squash-merging via PUT /pulls/N/merge without explicit commit_title, GitHub uses the PR title as the merge commit subject. If the PR title has camelCase, the resulting merge commit violates subject-case in commitlint, but the PR-side commitlint check (which lints git commit messages, not PR title) had already passed. Adding commitlint-main as required catches this on the post-merge push to main.

Replaced lint-commits / commitlint-main with lint-commits / commitlint, and made the job name in reusable-commitlint.yml static. The job was named commitlint-${{ head.ref || ref_name }}, so the published check context carried the branch name: commitlint-main only ever appeared on a push to main, never on a pull request. A required check that never reports leaves every PR stuck on 'Expected - Waiting for status to be reported', which forced an admin bypass on every merge - the exact thing the 2026-08-01 entry added strict checks to stop. The 2026-08-04 intent is not reachable this way regardless: required status checks gate the merge and are evaluated against the PR head SHA, so a check that only runs after the merge can never be a merge gate. The defense against the merge-commit-subject pitfall stays where it already worked, in the AGENTS.md section 4.5 checklist (validate the PR title, then pass commit_title and commit_message explicitly). The post-merge run still executes on main and still fails loudly if a bad subject lands.

Recorded why spark-match-07-article keeps statusChecks empty, so it reads as a decision rather than an oversight. Its CI workflow is path-filtered to **.tex, **.bib, figures/** and .github/workflows/**, because a pull request that only edits Markdown has nothing new to compile. A required check that a path filter can skip never reports, and GitHub then blocks the pull request forever on 'Expected - waiting for status to be reported'. That is the same failure mode as the commitlint ghost check in the entry above, reached by a different route: there the check name never matched, here the check never runs. The four pull requests merged into 07-article on 2026-08-06 all had an empty statusCheckRollup, which confirms it. Merge protection for that repository comes from the ruleset alone: one approving review, code-owner review required, linear history, squash-only. Making CI required would need the path filter dropped first, which means compiling the paper on every README typo.

Dropped refs/heads/dev from spark-match-07-article. That branch is abandoned: last commit 2026-07-10 against 2026-08-06 on main, no pull request has ever targeted it, and both of its workflows trigger only on main. Its 6 unique commits touch only .github/CODEOWNERS and .gitignore, and comparing those files directly shows .gitignore identical and CODEOWNERS differing only in comment lines, so nothing substantive is lost. Note the three-dot compare (main...dev) misleads here: it diffs against the merge base, not against the tip of main, so it appears to show unique work that main already superseded. Removing the ref is also what makes the branch deletable at all, since blockDeletion is true and the ruleset covered dev. The same abandoned pattern exists in spark-match-06-model-training (dev 2026-07-10, main 2026-07-26) and is left untouched pending that team's decision.

Declared the .github organization profile repository, which had never been in this manifest: it listed 9 repositories while the org has 10. This was not cosmetic. resolve_repos() passes --repos through verbatim, but the reconciler loop rejects an undeclared repository with not-in-manifest and continues before it reaches the legacy-protection block, so .github could not be reconciled and its classic branch protection could not be pruned even when named explicitly. Its ruleset already existed and already carried the shared name, but it was missing the deletion rule the defaults declare, so it had been drifting unmeasured. reviewerTeam is devops because the catch-all line in that repo's .github/CODEOWNERS is @spark-match/devops, which is what makes requireCodeOwnerReview reachable there.

What declaring .github costs, recorded as a decision rather than discovered later. Its classic protection on main sets require_last_push_approval=true and enforce_admins=true. The defaults here set requireLastPushApproval=false and adminBypassMode=pull_request, and configure-repo-rulesets.sh reads require_last_push_approval from .defaults only - there is no per-repository override for it - so reconciling .github and then pruning its classic layer drops last-push approval on main. Accepted for consistency: all 9 other repositories already run without it, and keeping .github as the single exception would mean either leaving a classic protection alive against the rulesets-plus-CODEOWNERS policy or adding a per-repo override to schema and script, which is a larger change than declaring a repository. The comment header in that repo's CODEOWNERS still describes the classic settings and will be stale once the prune runs. If last-push approval is wanted back, the fix is an override field, not a classic protection.

statusChecks for .github is empty on purpose, same reasoning as the spark-match-07-article entry above reached by a third route: that repository has zero workflows, so every required context would be a check that never reports and every pull request would sit forever on 'Expected - waiting for status to be reported'. refs keeps refs/heads/dev because the live protection covers it and removing a ref is what makes a branch deletable, but that branch is stale - last commit 2026-07-10 against 2026-07-27 on main, 4 ahead and 2 behind - which is the same abandoned shape as spark-match-06-model-training. Left in place for the same reason: dropping it is that team's call, not a side effect of declaring the repository.

Reconciled spark-match-02-infrastructure statusChecks against the live ruleset: 8 declared against 21 actually required, and the only repository of the ten reporting drift. The gap was not cosmetic. This manifest is what configure-repo-rulesets.sh writes, so running --apply on that repository would have replaced 21 gates with 8 and silently dropped every checkov-* matrix context - the governance tool weakening a repository by being used exactly as designed. The 14 checkov contexts were added to the ruleset by hand on 2026-08-01 and never came back here. Worse, four modules were not required at all: agent-service, ecr, frontend-hosting and oidc-frontend, which carry the ECS service, the container registry and the public CloudFront distribution, so the newest and least reviewed modules were also the least gated. lint-pr-title joins the list because with squash-only merges the pull request title becomes the commit subject and it is the only check that lints it. Checkov - the aggregate context Code Scanning derives from the SARIF - is deliberately NOT here: it was removed as required on 2026-08-04 because it goes NEUTRAL on large sync pull requests and blocks them forever, so re-adding it would have restored that trap. The list matches the 26 contexts published on pull request #199, obtained by diffing the ruleset against gh pr checks rather than by reading the workflows, which is the same method that found the gap.
